title: Ethylene selectivity in electrocatalytic CO2 reduction on Cu nanomaterials: a crystal phase-dependent study
abstract: Crystal phase of metal nanocatalysts significantly affects their catalytic performance. Cu-based nanomaterials are unique electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) to produce high-value hydrocarbons. However, studies to date are limited to the conventional face-centered cubic (fcc) Cu. Here, we report a crystal phase-dependent catalytic behavior of Cu, after the successful synthesis of high-purity 4H Cu and heterophase 4H/fcc Cu using the 4H and 4H/fcc Au as templates, respectively. Remarkably, the obtained unconventional crystal structures of Cu exhibit enhanced overall activity and higher ethylene (C2H4) selectivity in CO2RR compared to the fcc Cu. Density functional theory calculations suggest that the 4H phase and 4H/fcc interface of Cu favor the C2H4 formation pathway compared to the fcc Cu, leading to the crystal phase-dependent C2H4 selectivity. This study demonstrates the importance of crystal phase engineering of metal nanocatalysts for electrocatalytic reactions, offering a new strategy to prepare novel catalysts with unconventional phases for various applications.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Metal nanostructures possess intriguing catalytic activities in a wide range of electrochemical reactions.1-3 In particular, the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) stands out as a promising strategy to utilize the excess atmospheric CO2 for producing valuable chemicals.4-6 As known, Cu-based electrocatalysts are most efficient for CO2RR owing to their high energy density and the wide spectrum of useful products, such as carbon monoxide, formic acid, alcohols, and hydrocarbons like methane (CH4) and ethylene (C2H4).7-11 Recently, great interests have been attracted to unravel factors that can affect the CO2RR performance of metallic Cu or Cu-derived catalysts, such as the morphology,12-15 composition,16-19 valence state,20-23 doping,24 and surface functionalization25,26 of Cu, as well as special design of the CO2RR electrolyzer.27,28 However, all the Cu catalysts reported to date are based on the conventional facecentered cubic (fcc) crystal phase, i.e., the thermodynamically stable phase, and the effect of crystal phases of Cu on its catalytic behavior in CO2RR remains unknown.
As one important strategy for phase engineering of nanomaterials (PEN),29 crystal phase control over nanomaterials has emerged as an important approach to modulate the intrinsic catalytic activity of nanostructures.30-33 For instance, the unconventional fcc Ru was found to exhibit higher activity in electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) compared to the conventional hexagonal close-packed (hcp) Ru.34 Recently, the PtNi alloy nano-multipods demonstrated crystal phase-dependent HER activity, in which the nano-multipods with unconventional hcp phase outperforms their conventional fcc counterparts.35 Therefore, a novel synthetic strategy for unconventional crystal phases of Cu nanostructures is highly desired in order to explore their phasedependent performances in various applications, especially for the important CO2RR.
Recently, Au nanostructures with unconventional crystal phases, including Au nanoribbons (NRBs) with 4H phase,36 and
Au nanorods (NRs)37 with 4H/fcc heterophase have been synthesized. The 4H Au crystallizes in the characteristic stacking sequence of “ABCB” along the close-packed [001]4H direction,36 different from the thermodynamically stable fcc Au which features the stacking sequence of “ABC” along the closepacked [111]fcc direction. The heterophase 4H/fcc Au NRs feature the co-existing and randomly alternating of 4H and fcc phases along the [001]4H/[111]fcc directions.37 By using them as the templates, a universal wet-chemical approach has been developed to prepare the 4H phases and 4H/fcc heterophases of various metal nanostructures, such as Pt, Pd, Ag, Ru, Rh, Os, Ir and Cu, under mild conditions.37-39 However, due to the relatively large Au-Cu lattice mismatch (~12%), it still remains difficult for the wet-chemical synthesis of high-purity Cu nanostructures with unconventional crystal phase on either 4H Au NRBs or heterophase 4H/fcc Au NRs in high yield.
In this work, the phase-dependent catalytic performance of Cu in CO2RR is systematically investigated after the successful preparation of 4H Au@Cu and heterophase 4H/fcc Au@Cu core-shell nanostructures via a facile, epitaxial, wet-chemical approach under ambient conditions. Impressively, the unconventional structures of Cu, i.e., 4H Cu and 4H/fcc Cu, exhibit much higher catalytic activity and significantly improved C2H4 selectivity compared to the conventional fcc Cu. Theretical calculations reveal the intrinsically superior CO2RR activity and higher C2H4 selectivity of Cu with 4H phase and 4H/fcc heterophase, which are consistent with our experimental results.

sections.heading: Result and Discussion
sections.text:
After the heterophase 4H/fcc Au NRs (Figure S1) and 4H Au NRBs (Figure S2) were synthesized using our previous methods with slight modifications (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information),36,37 they were used as templates to epitaxially grow Cu shells to form 4H/fcc Au@Cu NRs (Scheme 1) and 4H Au@Cu NRBs, respectively (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Informgation). characterization of the unique crystal phase heterostructure, i.e., the heterophase 4H/fcc Au@Cu NRs. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image indicates the high-purity production (Figure 1a). Figure 1b and c confirm the uniform coating of Cu with an average thickness of 5.9 ± 0.9 nm on the 4H/fcc Au NRs (Figure 2c). The lattice difference between the Cu shell and the Au core results in the formation of Moiré pattern on top of the Au core (Figure 1c). To gain insight into the growth behavior of Cu, Cs-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) image was taken at the Au-Cu interface (Figure 1d). Two sets of diffraction spots in the fast Fourier transform (FFT) pattern of Figure 1d is observed (Figure 1e), suggesting that Cu and Au adopt the same crystal phase. The epitaxial relationship between Cu and Au was also proved by taking FFT patterns of the selected areas (f and g in Figure 1d), in which the characteristic diffraction patterns of 4H (along zone axis of [110]4H) and fcc (along zone axis of [101]fcc) phases were observed in Figure 1f and Figure 1g, respectively. The energy dispersion X-day spectroscopy (EDS) linear scan of Au and Cu elements across a representative Au@Cu NR (Figure 1h) show a typical core-shell profile (Figure 1i), further confirming the Au@Cu core-shell structure. Scheme 1. (a) Epitaxial growth of heterophase 4H/fcc Au@Cu core-shell NR under room temperature and (b) electrochemical CO2RR on 4H/fcc Au@Cu NR. Importantly, this wet-chemical approach can also be applied to prepare high-purity 4H Au@Cu NRBs (Figure 2, see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information). The SEM (Figure 2a), TEM (Figure 2b), and high-magnification TEM (Figure 2c) images show the high purity of as-obtained Au@Cu NRBs and the uniform coating of Cu shell with an average thickness of 6.7 ± 1.6 nm, comparable to that of Au@Cu NRs. Similarly, the Moiré pattern is also observed on the top of the Au core. The epitaxial growth of Cu on Au can be identified by the coherent Au-Cu lattice fringes at the Au-Cu interface (Figure 2d) and the corresponding FFT pattern (Figure 2e). The typical Au@Cu core-shell profile is confirmed by the EDS linear scan (Figure 2f,g). The crystal phases of the 4H/fcc Au@Cu NRs and 4H Au@Cu NRBs can also be identified by the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns (Figure S3), which match well the XRD patterns of their corresponding Au templates. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (Figure S4) is performed to confirm the metallic states of Au and Cu in the as-obtained Au@Cu nanostructures. Note that weak satellite peaks are observed along with the strong metallic Cu peaks, indicating the inevitable occurrence of the slight Cu oxidation under ambient conditions.
The Cu-based nanocatalysts are promising for electrocatalytic CO2RR due to their unique ability of converting CO2 into high-value hydrocarbons in aqueous solutions.40,41 Using the Au@Cu core-shell nanostructures with different crystal phases as catalysts, we systematically investigated the role of crystal phases of Cu on the electrochemical CO2RR. All measurements were conducted by constant-potential electrolysis, and the products were measured with on-line gas chromatographic analysis and off-line liquid chromatographic analysis (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information). In a control experiment, as shown in Figure S5, fcc Cu nanoparticles were synthesized for comparison on the electrochemical CO2RR. The loading amount of Cu was optimized based on the 4H/fcc Au@Cu NRs (Figure S6), which was kept same for all catalysts, i.e., 4H Au@Cu, 4H/fcc Au@Cu and fcc Cu, in the CO2RR. At potentials between -0.4 and -1.2 V (vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)), substantial reduction current densities (normalized to the geometric surface areas of electrodes) were observed on both 4H and 4H/fcc Au@Cu (Figure 3a). It suggests that both 4H and 4H/fcc Au@Cu exhibited stable electrocatalytic performance without any obvious loss of current densities over accumulated electrolysis for 9 h at the selected potentials (Figure 3a). More negative potentials led to the generation of C2H4 as the main product, accompanied with small amount of CH4. The main byproduct was H2, which was generated from the reduction of water. The highest overall Faradaic efficiency (FE) of CO2RR were ~88 % on 4H Au@Cu occurred at -0.75 V (vs RHE) and ~91 % on 4H/fcc Au@Cu at -0.82 V vs RHE), respectively. Under the same condition, fcc Cu exhibited lower selectivity for CO2RR compared to 4H and 4H/fcc Au@Cu with a highest overall FE of 84 % at -1.11 V (Figure S7). The onset potentials commencing CO2RR, as an indicator of the overall CO2RR catalytic activity, of 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu were found to be approximately 200 mV less negative (lower onset potential) than that of fcc Cu (Figure 3d). Since C2H4 possesses superior market value among the various reported products of CO2RR,42 the catalytic selectivity of the aforementioned three catalysts for C2H4 production was further investigated (Figure 3e). Using the 4H Au@Cu as catalyst, C2H4 was detected at potentials more negative than - 0.87 V. The FEC2H4 increased with more negative potentials and reached a maximum of 44.9 % at -1.11 V. A similar trend was found using the 4H/fcc Au@Cu as catalyst for the C2H4 production, and the FEC2H4 reached up to 46.7 % at -1.17 V. Such high C2H4 selectivities on 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu are among the best FEC2H4s reported on the metallic Cu catalysts for CO2RR (Table S1) and also comparable to those on nonmetallic Cu-based catalysts (Table S2). At the same experimental condition, fcc Cu showed the highest FEC2H4 of 41.1 %at -1.11 V, but its FEC2H4 decreased to 35.5 % at -1.17 V (Figure 3e). Furthermore, the partial current densities for the C2H4 production (jC2H4) on 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu are much higher than that on the fcc Cu at the similar potential (Figure 3f). The jC2H4 reached 14.4 mA cm-2 (at -1.11 V) on 4H Au@Cu and 21.0 mA cm-2 (at -1.17 V) on 4H/fcc Au@Cu, which are more than 3.6 times those on fcc Cu under similar potentials (3.9 mA cm-2 at -1.11 V, 5.8 mA cm-2 at -1.17 V). Such high jC2H4 values put 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu among the best reported metallic Cu catalysts for CO2RR tested under same conditions (Table S1). The partial current densities of all the products are shown in Figure S8. Additionally, the 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu possessed much smaller Tafel slopes of 112 mV dec−1 and 129 mV dec−1 for C2H4 production, respectively, compared to the fcc Cu (191 mV dec−1) (Figure S9), which suggests that the reaction kinetics of CO2 reduction to C2H4 on the 4H Au@Cu and 4H/fcc Au@Cu is faster than that on the fcc Cu. Moreover, to further compare their intrinsic catalytic activities for the CO2RR and C2H4 production, the current densities on 4H Au@Cu, 4H/fcc Au@Cu and fcc Cu are normalized to their electrochemical surface areas that are measured by the Pb underpotential deposition method (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information, Figure S10S11).43,44 The normalized jCO2RR and jC2H4 on 4H Au@Cu are still much higher compared to fcc Cu, while those on 4H/fcc Au@Cu are mostly in between, indicating that the unconventional 4H Cu possess higher intrinsic catalytic activity. Importantly, TEM images (Figure S12) the 4H Au@Cu NRBs and 4H/fcc Au@Cu NRs after the CO2RR measurement show no obvious morphology change, indicating their good structural stability. To gain insight into the crystal phase-dependent electrocatalytic behaviors, density functional theory (DFT) computations were performed on different surfaces of the Cu catalysts (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information, Figures S13-S16, Tables S3-S4), including 4H(110) and 4H(1 0) on the 4H Cu (Figure 2d-g), 4H(110), 1 4H(1 0) and the interface of 4H(110) and fcc(101) (denoted as 1 4H(110)/fcc(101)) on the 4H/fcc Cu (Figure 3d-e), as well as fcc(100), fcc(101) and fcc(111) on the fcc Cu.45,46 Free energy diagrams of the CO2 reduction indicate that the hydrogenation of CO2 into *COOH (reaction free energy denoted as ΔGCOOH) is the potential-determining step for producing CO on all the surfaces (Figure S14). The lower ΔGCOOH of 4H surfaces compared to most of the fcc surfaces (Figure S14) indicates that the 4H Cu exhibits an overall higher CO2RR activity than the fcc Cu, which also aligns well with the much lower onset potentials of 4H Cu and 4H/fcc Cu compared to fcc Cu (Figure 4d). To produce C2H4, the C-C coupling plays a key role. While several mechanisms for the C-C coupling pathway have been proposed based on the fcc Cu,47-52 in this work, C-C coupling via the reaction between *CO and *CHO intermediates is adopted (see Materials and Methods in Supporting Information, Figures S15-S16).5,47,48 Briefly, the formation of *COH intermediate mainly leads to the CH4 production, while the *CHO intermediate mainly leads to the formation of C2H4 through the coupling of *CO and *CHO.5,47,48 Therefore, the competition between the formation of *CHO and *COH is used to evaluate the C2H4 selectivity. The lower energy barrier for the formation of *COH compared to *CHO (Figure S16a) indicates that the formation of *COH is preferred on the fcc(111) facet, leading to the poor C2H4 selectivity. For the other 5 surfaces, i.e., fcc(100), fcc(101), 4H(110), 4H(1 0) and 1 4H(110)/fcc(101) interface, the formation of *CHO is more energetically favored (Figure S16a), resulting in the preferred C2H4 production via the exothermic coupling of *CO and *CHO (Figure S16b). Therefore, taking all the calculated surfaces into account, 4H Cu possesses overall higher C2H4 selectivity than does the fcc Cu, which is in good agreement with our experimental results (Figure 4e,f).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In conclusion, a facile method is developed to prepare 4H Au@Cu and heterophase 4H/fcc Au@Cu core-shell nanostructures with high purity under ambient conditions. The epitaxially grown 4H Cu and 4H/fcc Cu shells exhibit much greater CO2RR current densities and better C2H4 selectivity compared to those of fcc Cu, demonstrating the crystal phasedependent C2H4 selectivity of Cu, which aligns well with the theoretical calculation results. This study enables the rational design of Cu-based CO2RR catalysts via the crystal phase engineering of Cu, and also demonstrates a new strategy to prepare novel metal nanocatalysts for various promising applications.
